{{Short description|Criterion for positivity of a Hermitian matrix}}
In mathematics, '''Sylvester's criterion''' is a [[necessary and sufficient condition|necessary and sufficient]] criterion to determine whether a [[Hermitian matrix]] is [[Definite matrix|positive-definite]], due to [[James Joseph Sylvester]].

Sylvester's criterion states that a ''n'' × ''n'' Hermitian matrix ''M'' is positive-definite [[if and only if]] all the following matrices have a positive [[determinant]]:
* the upper left 1-by-1 corner of ''M'',
* the upper left 2-by-2 corner of ''M'',
* the upper left 3-by-3 corner of ''M'',
* <math>{}\quad\vdots</math>
* ''M'' itself.
In other words, all of the ''leading'' [[principal minor]]s must be positive. By using appropriate permutations of rows and columns of ''M'', it can also be shown that the positivity of ''any'' nested sequence of ''n'' principal minors of ''M'' is equivalent to ''M'' being positive-definite.<ref name="ref4"/>

An analogous theorem holds for characterizing [[positive-semidefinite matrix|positive-semidefinite]] Hermitian matrices, except that it is no longer sufficient to consider only the ''leading'' principal minors as illustrated by the Hermitian matrix
: <div class="center"><math>
\begin{pmatrix}
0&0&-1\\
0&-1&0\\
-1&0&0
\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{with eigenvectors}\quad
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\1\\0
\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\0\\1
\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{and}\quad
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\0\\-1
\end{pmatrix}.
</math></div>
A Hermitian matrix ''M'' is positive-semidefinite if and only if ''all'' [[principal minor]]s of ''M'' are nonnegative.<ref name="ref1b"/><ref name="prussing" />

== Proof for the case of positive definite matrices ==
Suppose <math>M_n</math> is <math>n\times n</math> Hermitian matrix <math>M_n^{\dagger}=M_n</math>. Let <math>M_k,k=1,\ldots n</math> be the leading principal minor matrices, i.e. the <math>k\times k</math> upper left corner matrices. It will be shown that if <math>M_n </math> is positive definite, then the principal minors are positive; that is, <math>\det M_k>0 </math> for all <math> k </math>.

<math>M_k</math> is positive definite. Indeed, choosing 
: <div class="center"><math> x=\left(
\begin{array}{c} x_1\\ \vdots\\ x_k\\ 0\\ \vdots\\0\end{array}
\right) = 
\left(
\begin{array}{c}
\vec{x}\\
0\\
\vdots\\
0
\end{array}
\right)
</math></div>
we can notice that <math>0<x^{\dagger} M_n x=\vec{x}^{\dagger}M_k\vec{x}. </math> Equivalently, the eigenvalues of <math>M_k</math> are positive, and this implies that <math>\det M_k>0</math> since the determinant is the product of the eigenvalues.

To prove the reverse implication, we use [[Mathematical induction|induction]]. The general form of an <math>(n+1) \times (n+1)</math> Hermitian matrix is
: <div class="center"><math>M_{n+1}= \left( \begin{array}{cc}M_n&\vec{v}\\ \vec{v}^{\dagger}&d\end{array}\right) \qquad (*)</math>,</div>

where <math>M_n</math> is an <math>n \times n</math> Hermitian matrix, <math>\vec{v}</math> is a vector and <math>d</math> is a real constant.

Suppose the criterion holds for <math>M_n</math>. Assuming that all the principal minors of <math>M_{n+1}</math> are positive implies that <math>\det M_{n+1}>0</math>, <math>\det M_n>0</math>, and that <math>M_n</math> is positive definite by the inductive hypothesis. Denote
: <div class="center"><math>x=\left( \begin{array}{c}\vec{x}\\ x_{n+1}\end{array} \right) </math></div>
then
: <math>x^{\dagger}M_{n+1}x=\vec{x}^{\dagger}M_n\vec{x}+x_{n+1}\vec{x}^{\dagger}\vec{v}+\bar{x}_{n+1}\vec{v}^{\dagger}\vec{x}+d|x_{n+1}|^2  </math>
By completing the squares, this last expression is equal to
: <math>(\vec{x}^{\dagger}+\vec{v}^{\dagger}M_n^{-1}\bar{x}_{n+1})M_n(\vec{x}+x_{n+1}M_n^{-1}\vec{v})-|x_{n+1}|^2\vec{v}^{\dagger}M_n^{-1}\vec{v}+d|x_{n+1}|^2 </math>
: <math>=(\vec{x}+\vec{c})^{\dagger}M_n(\vec{x}+\vec{c})+|x_{n+1}|^2(d-\vec{v}^{\dagger}M_n^{-1}\vec{v}) </math>
where <math>\vec{c}=x_{n+1}M_n^{-1}\vec{v}</math> (note that <math>M_n^{-1}</math> exists because the eigenvalues of <math>M_n</math> are all positive.) 
The first term is positive by the inductive hypothesis. We now examine the sign of the second term. By using the [[Block matrix#Block matrix operations|block matrix determinant formula]]
<div class="center"><math>\det \left(\begin{array}{cc}A&B\\C&D\end{array} \right)=\det A\det(D-CA^{-1}B)</math></div>

on <math>(*)</math> we obtain
: <math>\det M_{n+1}=\det M_n(d-\vec{v}^{\dagger}M_n^{-1}\vec{v})>0</math>, which implies <math>d-\vec{v}^{\dagger}M_n^{-1}\vec{v}>0</math>. 
Consequently, <math>x^{\dagger}M_{n+1}x>0.</math>

==Proof for the case of positive semidefinite matrices==
Let <math>M_n</math> be an ''n'' x ''n'' Hermitian matrix. Suppose <math>M_n</math> is semidefinite. Essentially the same proof as for the case that <math>M_n</math> is strictly positive definite shows that all principal minors (not necessarily the leading principal minors) are non-negative.

For the reverse implication, it suffices to show that if <math>M_n</math> has all non-negative principal minors, then for all ''t>0'', all leading principal minors of the Hermitian matrix <math>M_n+tI_n</math> are strictly positive, where <math>I_n</math> is the ''n''x''n'' [[identity matrix]]. Indeed, from the positive definite case, we would know that the matrices <math>M_n+tI_n</math> are strictly positive definite. Since the limit of positive definite matrices is always positive semidefinite, we can take <math>t \to 0</math> to conclude.

To show this, let <math>M_k</math> be the ''k''th leading principal submatrix of <math>M_n.</math> We know that <math>q_k(t) = \det(M_k + tI_k)</math> is a polynomial in ''t'', related to the characteristic polynomial <math>p_{M_k}(t)</math> via
<math display=block>q_k(t) = (-1)^kp_{M_k}(-t).</math> We use the identity in [[Characteristic polynomial#Properties]] to write
<math display=block>q_k(t) = \sum_{j=0}^k t^{k-j} \operatorname{tr}\left(\textstyle\bigwedge^j M_k\right),</math>
where <math display="inline">\operatorname{tr}\left(\bigwedge^j M_k\right)</math> is the trace of the ''j''th exterior power of <math>M_k.</math>

From [[Minor (linear algebra)#Multilinear algebra approach|the definition of minors]], we know that the entries in the matrix expansion of <math>\bigwedge^j M_k</math> (for ''j > 0'') are just the minors of <math>M_k.</math> In particular, the diagonal entries are the principal minors of <math>M_k</math>, which of course are also principal minors of <math>M_n</math>, and are thus non-negative. Since the trace of a matrix is the sum of the diagonal entries, it follows that <math display=block>\operatorname{tr}\left(\textstyle\bigwedge^j M_k\right) \geq 0.</math> Thus the coefficient of <math> t^{k-j}</math> in <math>q_k(t)</math> is non-negative for all ''j > 0.'' For ''j = 0'', it is clear that the coefficient is 1. In particular, <math>q_k(t) > 0</math> for all ''t > 0'', which is what was required to show.
